name: Ultherapy / HIFU skin tightening
summary: Clinic ultrasound device cleared for brow, neck and chest lifting; modest, gradual results and mostly small device studies.
lead: Ultherapy is a non-invasive cosmetic procedure that uses micro-focused ultrasound with visualization (MFU-V) to heat deep skin layers, with the aim of lifting and tightening skin on areas such as the brow, neck and under the chin. It is made by Ulthera, Inc., which Merz Aesthetics acquired in 2014. Other devices using high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) for skin tightening are sold under different names.

name: Thermage / monopolar RF
summary: Clinic radiofrequency heating for mild-to-moderate skin laxity; small studies report modest improvement.
lead: Thermage is a brand of non-ablative monopolar radiofrequency (RF) treatment used in clinics for skin tightening of the face, neck and eyelids. It heats the dermis with RF energy while the surface is cooled, with the aim of tightening lax skin and softening fine lines without surgery. The device was first sold as ThermaCool and is now marketed as Thermage FLX.

name: Profhilo / skin booster injectables
summary: Injectable hyaluronic acid sold as skin bio-remodelling; small studies report better hydration and elasticity, not volume.
lead: Profhilo is an injectable hyaluronic acid (HA) product made by IBSA Derma, launched in Europe in 2015, that is marketed as a skin 'bio-remodelling' treatment rather than a volume filler. Each syringe combines high and low molecular weight HA stabilised by a heat process, with no chemical cross-linker.

name: Rejuran / salmon DNA facial
summary: Polynucleotide (PN) skin-booster injections made from salmon DNA, sold as a skin-quality treatment; evidence for appearance use is still thin and mostly unpublished.
lead: A Rejuran or salmon DNA facial is a cosmetic procedure in which a polynucleotide (PN) preparation, derived from salmon DNA, is injected into or just beneath the skin to improve its quality. The best-known product name is Rejuran, and the ingredient is also referred to as polydeoxyribonucleotide (PDRN). It is promoted for skin texture, fine lines, under-eye skin and overall rejuvenation rather than for adding volume the way a conventional filler does.

name: PRP facial (vampire facial)
summary: Microneedling combined with your own platelet-rich plasma, popularised as the 'vampire facial'; controlled evidence for facial rejuvenation is limited and infection control is the main safety issue.
lead: A PRP facial, popularly known as a vampire facial, is a cosmetic procedure in which blood drawn from the patient is centrifuged to produce platelet-rich plasma (PRP), which is then applied to the face, most often together with microneedling. It is marketed for skin rejuvenation, fine lines, texture and acne scars.
claims: PRP microneedling can improve skin quality and slow visible ageing.
Doing PRP at home or in a self-run setup is a workable alternative to a clinic.

name: Mesotherapy
summary: Cocktail micro-injections into the skin, used for hair, skin and fat; supported by small studies in some uses, with limited standardisation and documented infection outbreaks from poor hygiene.
lead: Mesotherapy, also called local intradermal therapy, is a technique in which small doses of drugs, vitamins, minerals, enzymes, hyaluronic acid or plant extracts are injected through fine needles into the dermis or just beneath the skin. Its stated aim is localised action with minimal systemic exposure. A needle-free pressurised version delivers the ingredients with a jet of air.
claims: Scalp mesotherapy can regrow or thicken hair and may replace a transplant.
Mesotherapy cocktails dissolve fat or rejuvenate skin.
Mesotherapy is safe because it uses very small doses.

name: IPL photofacial
summary: Broad-spectrum light flashes used to treat sun spots, redness and broken capillaries; supported for pigment and vascular concerns, less so for wrinkles.
lead: An IPL photofacial, also called photorejuvenation, is a cosmetic and dermatological treatment that uses intense pulsed light (IPL) to improve skin affected by sun damage, uneven pigmentation, redness and visible small blood vessels. A computer-controlled handheld flashlamp emits brief pulses of non-coherent, broad-spectrum light, roughly 400 to 1200 nm, which targets melanin, haemoglobin and water in the skin.

name: Plasma pen (fibroblasting)
summary: A handheld device that arcs ionised gas onto the skin, marketed for eyelid and skin tightening; no controlled trials for cosmetic tightening were found.
lead: A plasma pen is a handheld device that generates a small electrical arc of ionised gas, or plasma, between its tip and the skin. Marketed in cosmetics as fibroblasting or a plasma lift, it is promoted for tightening loose skin, particularly on the eyelids, and for smoothing lines and removing small blemishes.
claims: A plasma pen can tighten eyelids and give 'baby-skin'.
Home plasma pens at $40-60 are an economical substitute for $400-1,900 clinic treatments.

name: Platysma Botox (Nefertiti lift)
summary: Botulinum toxin injected along the jawline and neck bands to soften platysmal cords and sharpen the lower-face contour; described in published case series and small trials, with temporary, modest results.
lead: The Nefertiti lift is a non-surgical cosmetic procedure in which botulinum toxin type A is injected into the platysma muscle, including vertical neck bands and the lower border of the mandible, to relax the muscle and reduce its downward pull on the lower face. It aims to soften platysmal bands and produce a subtle lift and sharper definition of the jawline.

name: Facial cupping
summary: Small suction cups glided over the face to lift and depuff; popular as a self-care ritual, with almost no face-specific research behind it.
lead: Facial cupping is the application of small suction cups to the skin of the face, usually with a light, gliding or brief-hold technique, with the aim of improving circulation, lifting or toning the skin, or reducing the appearance of sagging and puffiness. It is an area-based variant of cupping therapy, a traditional practice in which suction draws skin and soft tissue into a cup .

name: Face taping (Frownies / sleep patches)
summary: Paper or tape patches worn overnight to hold expression lines flat; a 130-year-old idea with no published trials.
lead: Face taping is the practice of applying adhesive patches or tape to areas of expression lines, such as the forehead, the vertical lines between the eyebrows and the corners of the eyes and mouth, usually overnight, to hold the skin flat and discourage the underlying muscles from creasing it. The best-known product is Frownies, an American brand of paper patches with a water-activated adhesive .

name: Lymphatic drainage facial massage
summary: Gentle face and neck massage meant to depuff; the technique is real, but cosmetic facial evidence is absent.
lead: Lymphatic drainage facial massage is a light, rhythmic, hands-on or tool-assisted massage of the face and neck intended to move lymph fluid, with the aim of reducing puffiness and giving a more defined, 'depuffed' appearance. It draws on manual lymphatic drainage (MLD), a gentle skin technique developed in the 1930s .

name: Topical estrogen (estriol) cream
summary: A weak estrogen cream discussed for skin thickness; menopausal skin data exist, appearance-use data are thin.
lead: Estriol (E3) is a weak natural estrogen, one of the three major endogenous estrogens alongside estradiol and estrone, and is available as a medication mainly for menopausal hormone therapy. It is sold as tablets, vaginal creams and suppositories, and some skin creams, some over the counter and some from compounding pharmacies .

name: Topical rapamycin
summary: Rapamycin creams for skin aging; approved for a rare facial condition, with only one small exploratory aging trial.
lead: Rapamycin, also called sirolimus, is a macrolide compound first isolated in 1972 from bacteria in soil samples from Easter Island (Rapa Nui). It inhibits the protein mTOR and is approved as an oral immunosuppressant for transplant patients and for the lung disease lymphangioleiomyomatosis . Topical formulations are approved for facial angiofibromas in tuberous sclerosis complex (the FDA approved a sirolimus gel in 2022 and the EU authorised Hyftor in 2023) .

name: Quit smoking / vaping
summary: Giving up tobacco to avoid 'smoker's face'; the aging link is observational, and quitting-for-looks trials are missing.
lead: In looksmaxxing and skincare discussions, quitting smoking or vaping is cited as a way to avoid or slow smoking-related facial aging. 'Smoker's face' is the term for facial changes seen in many long-term smokers, including a pattern of wrinkles, sagging and a dull, yellowish or grayish complexion .

name: Sleeping on your back
summary: Sleeping face-up to dodge pillow creases; the wrinkle benefit has not been tested in trials.
lead: Sleeping on your back (the supine position) is a sleep posture that some looksmaxxing practitioners adopt in the belief that it avoids so-called sleep lines, the facial creases attributed to pressing the face into a pillow or mattress for hours each night.

name: Bee venom / snake peptide (Syn-Ake) creams
summary: Venom-mimic creams sold as topical Botox alternatives; only lab data exist.
lead: Bee venom and Syn-Ake creams are cosmetics that borrow from venoms: bee venom products use honeybee venom or its components, while Syn-Ake is a synthetic peptide marketed as a topical alternative to botulinum toxin for wrinkles, named for its design as a mimic of a snake-venom peptide.

name: Sunscreen-maxxing
summary: Daily SPF and strict reapplication; the most evidence-backed anti-photoageing habit in the wiki's sources.
lead: Sunscreen-maxxing is the looksmaxxing term for strict daily use of sunscreen, with regular reapplication, to limit ultraviolet exposure and the skin ageing attributed to it.

name: Tretinoin protocol (tret, buffering)
summary: Slow-ramped, moisturiser-buffered prescription retinoid use; tretinoin itself is well studied, the buffering routine is not.
lead: The tretinoin protocol, often shortened to "tret" in forums, refers to the way looksmaxxing practitioners introduce and use topical tretinoin, a prescription retinoid, typically by increasing use slowly and sometimes "buffering" it with moisturiser to reduce irritation.

name: Hydrogen water / topical hydrogen
summary: Hydrogen-infused drinks and creams sold on antioxidant claims; the evidence for appearance is thin.
lead: Hydrogen water and topical hydrogen products are drinks and skincare items infused with molecular hydrogen (H2), promoted in some wellness and anti-ageing circles for antioxidant effects on skin and the body.

name: Placenta / sheep placenta creams
summary: Animal placenta extract creams sold for anti-ageing; no clinical evidence was found.
lead: Placenta creams are topical skincare products containing extracts of animal placenta, most often from sheep, marketed for skin regeneration, moisturisation and reduced wrinkles.

name: Pulsed dye laser / V-beam for redness
summary: A clinic vascular laser that targets hemoglobin in visible blood vessels; long established for birthmarks and used for facial redness and broken capillaries, with temporary bruising a common trade-off.
lead: A pulsed dye laser (PDL) is a medical laser that emits yellow light, commonly at 595 nm, which is strongly absorbed by oxyhemoglobin in blood vessels. The Vbeam family made by Candela Medical is the best-known branded line . Clinicians use PDLs for port-wine stains, hemangiomas, facial and leg telangiectasias, rosacea-related redness and some scars .

name: Hydrafacial
summary: A branded in-clinic cleansing and exfoliating facial that uses suction and serums; popular and low-downtime, with only a small published evidence base.
lead: Hydrafacial is a branded facial treatment that combines cleansing, chemical exfoliation, suction-based extraction and serum application using a single handheld device. It is commonly described as a form of hydradermabrasion, which encyclopedias class as a type of microdermabrasion using water-based sprays and a textured tip .

name: Metronidazole / ivermectin (rosacea creams)
summary: Prescription topicals for the bumps and inflammation of rosacea; clinicians rate them well-studied, but they do little for persistent flat redness.
lead: Topical metronidazole and topical ivermectin are two prescription creams or gels used for the inflammatory form of rosacea. Metronidazole is a nitroimidazole antimicrobial developed by Rhône-Poulenc and first marketed in France in 1960 . Ivermectin was discovered through work by Satoshi Ōmura and William Campbell, who shared part of the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for it, and the 1% cream is sold as Soolantra for rosacea .

name: Brimonidine gel (Mirvaso)
summary: A prescription vasoconstrictor gel approved in 2013 for facial redness in rosacea; it works within hours but is temporary, and rebound redness has been reported.
lead: Brimonidine gel (Mirvaso, brimonidine tartrate 0.33%) was approved by the US FDA in 2013 for facial erythema of rosacea and was described at launch as the first drug aimed at the hallmark redness of the condition . Brimonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist, first patented in 1972 and in medical use since 1996 for eye conditions .

name: Oxymetazoline cream (Rhofade)
summary: A prescription vasoconstrictor cream approved in 2017 for persistent facial redness of rosacea; it narrows vessels for a temporary reduction in redness.
lead: Oxymetazoline cream (brand name Rhofade) is a topical 1% formulation of the alpha-adrenergic agonist oxymetazoline, approved by the US FDA in January 2017 for persistent facial erythema associated with rosacea in adults . It is a vasoconstrictor intended to reduce visible redness .

name: Glass skin routine
summary: A K-beauty goal of poreless, translucent, glowing skin pursued through a multi-step routine; online it is as much an aesthetic ideal as a defined protocol, with no dedicated clinical studies.
lead: Glass skin is a skincare ideal, originating in Korean beauty culture and spread on social media, of skin that looks smooth, pore-minimal and translucent with a dewy sheen. The term describes both the look and the multi-step routine used to pursue it.
claims: Glass skin is achievable through a layered K-beauty routine.
Specific foods and heavy water intake produce clearer, glassy skin.

name: Low-glycemic / anti-inflammatory diet
summary: Eating low-GI and cutting sugar or dairy for clearer skin; acne trials are encouraging for glycemic load, but a full 'anti-inflammatory' diet is untested for looks.
lead: A low-glycemic or anti-inflammatory diet, in looksmaxxing and skincare circles, is an eating pattern chosen with the aim of clearing acne and reducing facial redness or puffiness. It generally means favouring foods with a low glycemic index (GI) and limiting refined sugars, and is sometimes combined with reducing dairy or processed foods.

name: Facial steaming / sauna
summary: Heat and steam sessions for a skin 'glow'; sauna has health research, but nothing on facial appearance.
lead: Facial steaming and sauna sessions are heat-based practices that some people use in pursuit of a 'glow', often described as flushed, hydrated or cleansed-looking skin. Facial steaming typically involves directing warm vapour at the face, and commercial steamers and bath hoods exist for the purpose.

name: Hydration / water chugging
summary: Drinking gallons of water for glowy skin; no trials back the appearance claim, and overdrinking has its own documented risk.
lead: Hydration or 'water chugging' refers to deliberately drinking large amounts of water, sometimes gallons per day, in the belief it produces clearer, plumper or 'glowy' skin. It is a common lifestyle suggestion in skincare and appearance communities.
